content: Rennet is a natural complex of enzymes produced in the stomachs of mammals to aid in the digestion of their mother's milk. It contains a proteolytic enzyme, also known as a protease, which coagulates milk by separating it into solid curds and liquid whey. This process is facilitated by enzymes such as chymosin, pepsin, or lipase. Non-animal sources of rennet substitutes are also available. The primary use of rennet is in the production of cheese, curd, and junket. Chymosin specifically interacts with κ-casein, cleaving the protein between the amino acids phenylalanine (position 105) and methionine (position 106). This cleavage results in two fragments: a soluble fragment (residues 106–169), which becomes part of the whey and is known as glycomacropeptide, containing glycosylation sites for κ-casein, and an insoluble fragment (residues 1–105). In the presence of calcium ions, the insoluble fragment causes the coagulation of casein micelles, forming curds. Natural calf rennet is extracted from the inner mucosa of the fourth stomach chamber (the abomasum) of young calves. These stomachs are a by-product of veal production. Rennet extracted from older calves, which are grass-fed or grain-fed, contains less or no chymosin but higher levels of pepsin. Such rennet is suitable only for specific types of milk and cheeses. Each ruminant species produces a unique type of rennet tailored to digest its mother's milk. For example, kid-goat rennet is used for goat's milk, and lamb rennet is used for sheep's milk. Rennet or digestive enzymes from other animals, such as swine pepsin, are not used in cheese production, although swine pepsin is employed in protein disulfide bond analysis. In traditional methods, dried and cleaned stomachs of young calves are sliced into small pieces and soaked in saltwater or whey, along with vinegar or wine to lower the pH of the solution. After soaking for a period (overnight or several days), the solution is filtered. The crude rennet remaining in the filtered solution can then be used to coagulate milk. Approximately 1 gram of this solution can coagulate 2000 to 4000 grams of milk. This method is now primarily used by traditional cheesemakers in regions such as Switzerland, Jura (France), Romania, and the Alpine regions of Austria. In modern methods, deep-frozen stomachs are milled and placed in an enzyme-extracting solution. The crude rennet extract is activated by adding acid, as the enzymes in the stomach are initially produced in an inactive pre-form and are activated by stomach acid. After neutralizing the acid, the rennet extract undergoes multiple filtration stages and is concentrated to achieve the desired potency, typically around 1:15000 (1 kilogram of rennet can coagulate 15000 liters of milk). Preservatives are added to maintain stability. Due to the limited availability of suitable stomachs for rennet production, cheesemakers have explored alternative methods to coagulate milk. Artificial coagulants are a viable alternative, particularly for inexpensive or lower-quality cheeses. Since coagulation relies on enzymatic activity, the challenge has been to identify enzymes capable of cleaving casein in a manner that produces a taste and texture similar to animal-based rennet. Vegetable rennet is derived from plants with coagulating properties, such as fig tree bark, nettles, thistles, mallow, and creeping charlie. Enzymes from thistle or Cynara are used in traditional cheese production in the Mediterranean. These true vegetable rennets are suitable for vegetarians. While vegetable rennet may be used in kosher cheese production, most kosher cheeses are made with microbial rennet or genetically modified (GM) rennet. There is no industrial-scale production of vegetable rennet worldwide. Commercially labeled vegetable rennets often contain rennet derived from the mold Mucor miehei, which is classified as microbial rennet. Microbial rennet is produced by molds such as Rhizomucor miehei, which generate proteolytic enzymes. These molds are cultivated in fermenters, and the enzymes are concentrated and purified to prevent contamination with undesirable by-products. However, governmental food safety organizations, such as the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), do not grant Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS) status to enzymes produced by these molds. Cheeses made with microbial rennet often develop a bitter taste, especially after prolonged maturation. Microbial rennets are suitable for vegetarians, provided no animal-based feed was used during production. Genetically engineered rennet was developed to address the limitations of microbial rennets. With advancements in genetic engineering, calf genes were introduced into bacteria, fungi, or yeast to enable them to produce chymosin. Chymosin produced by genetically modified organisms was the first artificially produced enzyme to be approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Hard cheeses made with genetically engineered chymosin are now common. One example of a commercially available genetically engineered rennet is Chymax, developed by Pfizer. Today, the most widely used genetically engineered rennet is produced by the fungus Aspergillus niger. Issues related to aflatoxins and antibiotic-resistant marker genes have been resolved. Cheese production using genetically engineered rennet is similar to that using natural calf rennet. However, genetic rennet contains only one of the main chymosin types (either type A or type B), whereas natural rennet contains additional chymosin types. This distinction allows for the identification of the coagulant used in cheese production through specialized analysis of cleaved and uncleaved bonds. Often, a mixture of genetically engineered chymosin and natural pepsin is used to replicate the complexity of natural rennet and achieve similar coagulation, flavor, and taste development. Genetically modified rennets are suitable for vegetarians if no animal-based feed was used during fermentation, but only for vegetarians who accept GM-derived foods. Acid coagulation, such as with citric acid, is another method sometimes used in the production of inexpensive mozzarella without cheese maturation. Paneer is also made using this method. Acidification can also result from bacterial fermentation, as seen in cultured milk.
